title: The four tones
blurb: Pitch changes the word — mā, má, mǎ, mà are four different words.

cards.h: Pitch is part of the word
cards.body: In Mandarin the melody of a syllable is as important as its consonants and vowels. Say the same syllable with four different pitches and you get four unrelated words — nothing else changes.
Tone 1 is high and flat — hold one pitch like humming. Tone 2 rises like asking "huh?". Tone 3 dips low then rises. Tone 4 falls fast and hard, like a short command.
Some syllables carry no tone of their own. They're short, light, and borrow their pitch from the syllable before them. Numbered pinyin marks this with a 5.
When a syllable has more than one vowel letter, the mark goes on a or e first; in ou it goes on o; otherwise it goes on the last vowel written.

items.q: Which tone do you hear?
items.rv: mā — 妈 mother — tone 1, high and flat

items.q: Which tone do you hear?
items.rv: má — 麻 hemp — tone 2, rising

items.q: Which tone do you hear?
items.rv: mǎ — 马 horse — tone 3, low and dipping

items.q: Which tone do you hear?
items.rv: mà — 骂 scold — tone 4, falling sharply

items.q: In 你好吗 (nǐ hǎo ma), what tone is 吗?
items.rv: 吗 (ma) is always a light, toneless question particle

items.q: 好 is written hǎo, not hoǎ. Why does the mark sit on a?
opts: a and e always take priority over other vowels
the mark always goes on the last vowel
the mark always goes on the first vowel
items.a: a and e always take priority over other vowels
items.rv: Rule: a/e first, then ou → o, otherwise the last vowel

items.q: 都 is written dōu. Where does the tone mark go in the combination 'ou'?
items.rv: ou is a special case: the mark always lands on o

items.q: Which tone falls sharply from high to low, like a sharp command?
items.rv: Tone 4 is the fast falling tone

title: Simple finals: a o e i u ü
blurb: Six pure vowel sounds — including the tricky ü.

cards.body: These are the building blocks every other final is made from. Say each one on its own before you try it in a word.
rows: to go — ü, written u after q

cards.body: Round your lips like you're about to say u, but keep your tongue where it is for i. That combination is ü. English has no equivalent — most learners' first mistake is swapping it for u.

items.q: What is the final in 我 (wǒ)?
items.rv: 我 = w + o

items.q: What is the final in 喝 (hē)?
items.rv: 喝 = h + e

items.q: What is the final in 你 (nǐ)?
items.rv: 你 = n + i

items.q: What is the final in 不 (bù)?
items.rv: 不 = b + u

items.q: What is the final in 去 (qù)?
items.rv: 去 is spelled qu but pronounced with ü — after q the dots are dropped

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 绿 (lǜ) — rounded lips, tongue at the i position

items.q: After j, q, or x, how is ü written?
items.rv: The dots are dropped: ju, qu, xu are all really ü sounds

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 女 (woman)?
items.rv: 女 keeps its umlaut because it has no j/q/x before it

title: Initials: b p m f · d t n l
blurb: Aspiration — the puff-of-air test that splits b/p and d/t.

cards.body: b and p use the same lip position — the only difference is a puff of air. b has none, p has a strong burst. Hold a hand or tissue in front of your mouth: it barely moves for b, but jumps for p. The same pairing applies to d/t.
rows: dad — b, no puff of air
to fear — p, puff of air
big — d, no puff of air
he / she — t, puff of air

cards.body: m and n are nasal — air goes through the nose, lips closed for m, tongue tip on the ridge behind the teeth for n. f is like English f. l is a clear tongue-tip l, always light, never the 'dark l' at the end of English 'ball'.
rows: you — tongue tip on the ridge

items.q: Which initial do you hear?
items.rv: b — no puff of air

items.q: Which initial do you hear?
items.rv: p — strong puff of air

items.q: Which initial do you hear?
items.rv: d — no puff of air

items.q: Which initial do you hear?
items.rv: t — strong puff of air

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 你 (nǐ) — tongue tip on the ridge, nasal

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 'meal'?
items.rv: 饭 is fàn — f like English f

items.q: Which initial does 来 (lái) start with?
items.rv: 来 (lái) — clear, light l

items.q: Hold a tissue in front of your mouth. Which sound makes it flutter?
items.rv: p is aspirated: a burst of air follows the lip release

title: g k h · the three sibilant rows
blurb: z c s vs. zh ch sh r vs. j q x — the classic trap for English speakers.

cards.body: These come from the back of the throat, like English g, k, h, but crisper.
rows: can, as in 可以 — k

cards.body: z c s sit with the tongue tip flat behind the lower teeth, like a soft English 'ds/ts/s'. zh ch sh r curl the tongue tip back without touching anything — the single hardest sound for English speakers to place. j q x are flat and forward, always followed by i or ü, close to English 'j/ch/sh' but lighter.
rows: to eat — ch, tongue curled back
to be — sh, tongue curled back
sun / day — r, tongue curled back
thank, as in 谢谢 — x, flat and forward

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 吃 (chī) — retroflex, tongue curled back with a puff of air

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 是 (shì) — retroflex sh, tongue curled back

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 七 (qī) — flat, forward tongue, always before i/ü

items.q: j, q, and x can only be followed by which vowels?
items.rv: This row exists only before i and ü — no jia-without-i, no qa, no xo

items.q: Which initial does 这 (zhè) start with?
items.rv: 这 (zhè) — retroflex zh

items.q: Which initial does 在 (zài) start with?
items.rv: 在 (zài) — flat-tongue z

items.q: Which initial does 家 (jiā) start with?
items.rv: 家 (jiā) — flat, forward j

items.q: For zh, ch, sh, r, where does the tongue tip go?
opts: flat against the back of the teeth
pressed to the roof at the front
items.rv: Retroflex sounds: tongue curls back into the mouth, floating

title: Compound finals: ai ei ao ou · ia ie ua uo üe
blurb: Two vowel sounds glide smoothly into one syllable.

cards.body: Each of these is a smooth slide from the first vowel sound toward the second — don't pause in the middle. Say them slowly at first, then speed up until it's one motion.
rows: to study — üe, written ue after x

items.q: Which final does 白 (bái) have?
items.rv: 白 (bái) — ai glide

items.q: Which final does 好 (hǎo) have?
items.rv: 好 (hǎo) — ao glide

items.q: Which final does 都 (dōu) have?
items.rv: 都 (dōu) — ou glide

items.q: Which final does 写 (xiě) have?
items.rv: 写 (xiě) — ie glide

items.q: 学 is spelled xue. What is its final actually pronounced as?
items.rv: After x the ü loses its dots but keeps its sound

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 'many' (duō)?
items.rv: 多 is duō — u glides into o

items.q: Which final does 话 (huà) have?
items.rv: 话 (huà) — ua glide

items.q: In 好 (hǎo), which letter carries the tone mark?
items.rv: a always outranks o for the tone mark

title: Nasal finals: an en ang eng ong
blurb: -n touches the tongue tip; -ng doesn't touch anything.

cards.body: For -n, the tongue tip presses against the ridge behind your upper teeth, same as English 'n'. For -ng, the tongue tip touches nothing — the back of the tongue rises and the sound is nasal, like English 'sing'. Mixing these up is one of the most common mistakes for English speakers.
rows: friend, as in 朋友 — eng

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 慢 (màn) — tongue tip touches the ridge

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 忙 (máng) — tongue tip touches nothing

items.q: Which final does 红 (hóng) have?
items.rv: 红 (hóng) — ong, lips rounded

items.q: For -ng, does the tongue tip touch the roof of the mouth?
items.rv: -ng is made entirely with the back of the tongue

items.q: Which final does 门 (mén) have?
items.rv: 门 (mén) — en, tongue tip touches the ridge

items.q: Which final does 朋 (péng) have?
items.rv: 朋 (péng) — eng, tongue tip touches nothing

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 'busy' (máng)?
items.rv: 忙 is máng

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 门 (mén) ends in -n, not -ng

title: i-row finals: ian in iang ing iong iao iu
blurb: Adding nasal and glide endings onto i.

cards.body: These finals all start from the i sound and add a nasal or glide ending. Watch the -n/-ng pairs again: ian vs iang, in vs ing.
rows: name, as in 名字 — ing

items.q: Which final does 天 (tiān) have?
items.rv: 天 (tiān) — ian

items.q: Which final does 心 (xīn) have?
items.rv: 心 (xīn) — in, tongue tip touches the ridge

items.q: Which final does 两 (liǎng) have?
items.rv: 两 (liǎng) — iang

items.q: Which final does 名 (míng) have?
items.rv: 名 (míng) — ing, back of the tongue only

items.q: 九 (jiǔ) is really 'jiou' shortened to what spelling?
items.rv: iou shortens to iu when written; the tone mark lands on u

items.q: Which final does 小 (xiǎo) have?
items.rv: 小 (xiǎo) — iao

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 心 (xīn) ends in -n

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 名 (míng) ends in -ng

title: u/ü-row finals and spelling shortcuts
blurb: uai ui uan un uang üan ün, plus the y/w and jqx spelling rules.

cards.body: Two of these are shortened in writing: uei becomes ui, and uen becomes un. Say the full form once, then the short written form — the sound doesn't change.
rows: whole, entire — üan written uan after q
skirt — ün written un after q

cards.h: No bare vowels: the y/w rule
cards.body: A syllable can't start with a naked i, u, or ü — pinyin adds y or w in front instead. i alone becomes yi, u alone becomes wu, ü alone becomes yu.

items.q: 对 (duì) is really 'duei' shortened to what spelling?
items.rv: uei shortens to ui; the tone mark lands on i

items.q: 春 (chūn) is really 'chuen' shortened to what spelling?
items.rv: uen shortens to un after an initial consonant

items.q: 全 (quán) — why are there no dots over the u?
opts: ü is written u after j, q, x
q can't be followed by ü
items.a: ü is written u after j, q, x
items.rv: quán is really qüán — the umlaut is dropped but the ü sound stays

items.q: 一 (yī) — why does it start with y instead of a bare i?
opts: pinyin syllables can't start with a bare i
items.a: pinyin syllables can't start with a bare i
items.rv: i, u, and ü always get a y/w when they start a syllable alone

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 五 (five)?
items.rv: 五 is wǔ — bare u becomes wu

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 雨 (rain)?
items.rv: 雨 is yǔ — bare ü becomes yu

items.q: Which final does 快 (kuài) have?
items.rv: 快 (kuài) — uai

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 短 (duǎn) ends in -n, not -ng

title: Special syllables: zhi chi shi ri zi ci si · er
blurb: The 'i' here is a buzz, not a real vowel — plus 儿 and erhua.

cards.body: After zh ch sh r z c s, the written i is not the vowel you hear elsewhere. It's just a buzzing continuation of the consonant — the tongue never moves to make a separate vowel sound.
rows: to know, as in 知道

cards.body: 儿 (ér) is a syllable on its own, made with the tongue curled back. Attached to the end of another syllable it becomes 'erhua' — the two blend into one sound with a retroflex color, common in Beijing speech.
rows: a little — diǎn + r blend into one syllable

items.q: In zhī, chī, shī, what is the 'i' sound really doing?
opts: it's just a buzz — the tongue stays where it is for the consonant
items.a: it's just a buzz — the tongue stays where it is for the consonant
items.rv: This i is a placeholder vowel, unlike i in nǐ or jiā

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 字 (zì) — flat tongue, not retroflex

items.q: Which is the correctly spelled pinyin for 二 (two)?
items.rv: 二 is èr — tongue curled back for the whole syllable

items.q: 一点儿 sounds like one syllable ending in what?
items.rv: Erhua fuses the r into the syllable before it

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 知 (zhī) — retroflex zh

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 词 (cí) — flat tongue c, not retroflex

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 是 (shì) — retroflex sh

items.q: Which word do you hear?
items.rv: 日 (rì) — retroflex r, no English equivalent

title: Tone sandhi: 3rd+3rd, 不, 一
blurb: Some tones change in speech but stay the same on the page.

cards.body: When a 3rd tone is immediately followed by another 3rd tone, the first one is actually spoken as a 2nd tone. The pinyin is still written with both as 3rd tone marks — only the pronunciation shifts.
rows: hello — written nǐ hǎo, spoken ní hǎo
very good — written hěn hǎo, spoken hén hǎo

cards.body: 不 is normally 4th tone. But when the next syllable is also 4th tone, 不 shifts to 2nd tone (bú) to avoid two hard falls in a row. Before any other tone it stays bù.
rows: don't eat — chī is 1st tone, so bù stays
not correct — duì is 4th tone, so bù → bú

cards.body: 一 is 1st tone when counting, at the end of a word, or as an ordinal. Before a 4th-tone syllable it becomes yí (2nd tone). Before a 1st-, 2nd-, or 3rd-tone syllable it becomes yì (4th tone).
rows: one (measure word) — gè is 4th tone, so yī → yí
one day — tiān is 1st tone, so yī → yì

items.q: How is 你好 actually pronounced?
items.rv: Two 3rd tones in a row: the first becomes 2nd tone in speech

items.q: 很好 (hěn hǎo) is actually spoken as?
items.rv: Same rule: 3rd+3rd → 2nd+3rd when spoken

items.q: 不对 (bù duì) — how is 不 actually pronounced here?
items.rv: 不 shifts to 2nd tone before another 4th-tone syllable

items.q: 不吃 (bù chī) — how is 不 actually pronounced here?
items.rv: 不 stays 4th tone before a non-4th-tone syllable

items.q: 一个 (yí ge) — what tone does 一 change to before this 4th-tone word?
items.rv: 一 becomes 2nd tone before a 4th-tone syllable

items.q: 一天 (yì tiān) — what tone does 一 change to before this 1st-tone word?
items.rv: 一 becomes 4th tone before a 1st-, 2nd-, or 3rd-tone syllable

items.q: When is 一 pronounced yī, unchanged?
opts: when counting, at the end of a word, or as an ordinal
items.a: when counting, at the end of a word, or as an ordinal
items.rv: Sandhi only applies when 一 is directly followed by another syllable

items.q: Does tone sandhi change how 你好 is written with tone marks?
opts: no — still written nǐ hǎo, only the spoken pitch shifts
items.a: no — still written nǐ hǎo, only the spoken pitch shifts
items.rv: Sandhi is a rule of speech, not of spelling

title: Neutral tone in words
blurb: 妈妈, 学生, 我们 — light, toneless syllables that lean on the one before.

cards.body: A neutral-tone syllable has no pitch contour of its own — it's short, light, and its exact pitch depends on the tone before it. In numbered pinyin it's written with a 5 and carries no tone mark in written pinyin.

items.q: Which syllable in 妈妈 is neutral tone?
items.rv: 妈妈 — the second mā loses its tone and becomes light

items.q: What tone is 生 in 学生 (xuésheng)?
items.rv: 生 carries no pitch of its own here — it's light and short

items.q: In numbered pinyin, neutral tone is written as which digit?
items.rv: xue2sheng5 — 5 marks the neutral tone

items.q: What tone is 们 in 我们 (wǒmen)?
items.rv: 们 is always neutral tone in this word

items.q: Which syllable in 谢谢 is neutral tone?
items.rv: The second xiè loses its falling tone and becomes light

items.q: What does a neutral-tone syllable sound like?
opts: short and light, its pitch shaped by the syllable before it
items.a: short and light, its pitch shaped by the syllable before it
items.rv: Neutral tone has no fixed contour of its own

items.q: What tone is 友 in 朋友 (péngyou)?
items.rv: 友 is neutral here, even though 友 alone is 3rd tone (yǒu)

items.q: 学生's numbered pinyin is xue2sheng__. What number fills the blank?
items.rv: 5 is the digit for neutral tone

title: Reading whole words: tone pairs
blurb: Two-syllable words fall into tone patterns — learn to hear the pair.

cards.body: Most Chinese words are two syllables, and each has its own tone pattern, like a two-note melody. Learn to hear the pattern as a whole instead of counting tones one at a time.

cards.h: Read the pattern, not the syllables
cards.body: When you see a new word, say each syllable's tone in your head first, then blend them smoothly — don't let the tone of the last syllable bleed backward onto the first.

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 你好?
items.rv: 你好 is written 3-3 — spoken sandhi makes it sound like 2-3, but the pattern is 3-3

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 中国?
items.rv: Zhōng (1) + guó (2)

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 学校?
items.rv: Xué (2) + xiào (4)

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 现在?
items.rv: Xiàn (4) + zài (4)

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 电脑?
items.rv: Diàn (4) + nǎo (3)

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 老师?
items.rv: Lǎo (3) + shī (1)

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 妈妈?
items.rv: Mā (1) + ma (neutral, 5)

items.q: What is the tone pattern of 谢谢?
items.rv: Xiè (4) + xie (neutral, 5)
